title: Partitioning-time dependent evolution of retained austenite and its impact on microstructure and mechanical properties in lean TRIP-assisted steel
abstract: TRIP-assisted multiphase steels are gradually finding employment in the automotive industry for their excellent strain-hardening characteristics. In the current study, in a comparatively lean composition steel, different combinations of multiple phases such as ferrite, austenite and martensite, were obtained by heat-treatment, consisting of Inter-critical annealing followed by partitioning treatment for different holding times. It was observed that, with increasing isothermal holding time, the volume fraction of retained austenite increases. Electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) and transmission electron microscope (TEM) studies revealed that during partitioning at 400°C, austenite decomposition occurs primarily by the growth of existing ferrite through interface migration, and also involved bainitic transformation features that are difficult to distinguish. As a consequence, the retained austenite is enriched with carbon and get stabilized against martensitic transformation at room temperature. The characteristics of the retained austenite was studied using in-situ high energy X-ray diffraction and differential scanning calorimetry. The mechanical properties have been found to be strongly influenced by the volume fraction of the microstructural constituents. The higher volume fraction of martensite has been observed to give rise to higher strength and the higher ductility is found to be related to higher amount of retained austenite. The mechanical balance between high strength and high ductility has been achieved with a high-volume fraction (around 20 %) of austenite. This comprehensive study implies that an adequate amount of retained austenite ensures the TRIP effect, while interaction among the phases present results in the achievement of excellent global mechanical properties.
journal: Journal of Alloys and Metallurgical Systems

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: In recent years, the global demand for lightweight and high-strength vehicles has grown significantly, driven by the dual goals of enhancing crash safety and reducing environmental CO₂ emissions  [1–3] . To meet these requirements, the development of advanced high-strength steels (AHSS) that exhibit both superior strength and excellent ductility has become critical. The concept of transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP), introduced by Zackay et al., offers a promising strategy to achieve this strength–ductility synergy  [4] . Effective utilization of the TRIP effect relies on the stabilization of the face-centered cubic (FCC) austenite phase at room temperature. Achieving this typically requires substantial additions of expensive alloying elements like Ni  [1,5]  and Mn  [2,6] , which poses cost-related challenges. Consequently, retaining a sufficient amount of stabilized austenite with minimized alloying additions remains a key hurdle in the practical implementation of TRIP steels in industrial applications.

Since the 1980s, significant research efforts, particularly within the automotive sector, have focused on developing cost-effective AHSS by exploiting the TRIP mechanism. These efforts have led to the emergence of low-alloyed TRIP-assisted steels  [7–11] . The microstructure of such steels typically consists of a combination of ferrite, retained austenite, bainite, and a minor amount of martensite  [8] . Their excellent mechanical performance is attributed to two primary mechanisms: The classical TRIP effect, wherein retained austenite transforms into martensite under strain, generating localized hardening that delays necking and extends uniform elongation  [4,12] . The complex mechanical interaction among the multiple phases, which enables redistribution of stress and strain across the microstructure, thereby enhancing the total plastic strain and work-hardening capacity  [13–15] . This highlights the importance of stabilizing an adequate volume fraction of retained austenite at room temperature to optimize the strength–ductility balance in low-alloy TRIP steels. Early studies have demonstrated that in lean-composition TRIP-assisted steels, approximately 5–15 % of austenite can be stabilized at room temperature using a relatively simple two-step heat treatment process  [16–18] . The first step involves intercritical annealing, during which ferrite and austenite phases coexist at a controlled temperature. The second step, known as partitioning, involves rapid cooling of the intercritically annealed samples to a temperature range of 350–450°C, followed by isothermal holding for a few minutes before cooling to room temperature. During this isothermal stage, part of the austenite transforms into bainitic ferrite, enriching the remaining austenite with carbon, which enhances its stability at room temperature  [19] . The alloying elements Si and Al, which have low solubility in cementite, play a key role in suppressing its formation within this temperature range  [20,21] . Both the volume fraction and stability of retained austenite are critical factors influencing the mechanical behavior of low-alloy TRIP steels  [22,23] . The stability of retained austenite its resistance to transformation into martensite is governed by several parameters: chemical composition  [16,24] , grain size  [25] , morphology  [22] , and the nature of surrounding phases  [26] . Among the stabilizing elements, Mn, Ni, and C are all effective, but carbon is the most potent stabilizer in lean-alloy steels. Austenite with less than 0.6 wt% carbon transforms to martensite under relatively low strain  [27] , while austenite containing more than 1.8 wt% carbon becomes overly stable and resists transformation  [28] . Therefore, a carbon content of approximately 1.0–1.8 wt% is considered optimal for promoting a progressive transformation during deformation, which is desirable for many industrial applications  [28] .

Grain size plays a crucial role: finer austenite grains (∼1 µm) resist martensitic transformation due to suppressed nucleation, while morphology also matters—blocky grains transform earlier than film-like (lath-type) ones. Regarding adjacent phases, Jacques et al. reported that austenite surrounded by ferrite experiences greater strain than when embedded in bainite  [29] , whereas Tomota et al. suggested ferrite provides stress relaxation, improving austenite stability  [13] . Despite extensive studies, no clear correlation exists between retained austenite fraction, stability, and mechanical properties, likely due to variations in intercritical annealing and partitioning parameters across different steel compositions. For example, Jacques et al. studied a low-Si steel (0.18C-0.39Si-1.33Mn wt%) annealed at 730°C and 780°C for 5 min: the lower temperature produced 25 % austenite (0.72 %C), while the higher yielded 75 % austenite (0.24 %C). Since high-carbon austenite shows lower M s  (∼200°C) than lean-carbon austenite (∼400°C), lower annealing temperatures are preferable for maximizing carbon enrichment. Appropriate annealing time is also critical to achieve equilibrium fractions without grain coarsening  [30] . Partitioning parameters further control austenite stability. Sugimoto et al.  [31]  showed that in 0.2C-1.5Mn-1.5Si steel, 5–12 % retained austenite formed at 425–475°C, with carbon enrichment increasing at lower temperatures. Longer holding (10–1000 s) promoted high-carbon austenite (1.4–1.65 %), though ferritic or bainitic transformations compete. Thus, microstructural evolution during partitioning critically determines retained austenite content and stability. Tailoring phase fractions remains key for balancing strength and ductility  [23,32] ; an optimum of 50–60 % ferrite, 5–15 % retained austenite, and the remainder bainite/martensite has been suggested  [33] . However, no consensus exists on precise measures to consistently achieve such optimized phase fractions.

Therefore, the objective of the present work is to investigate the influence of intercritical annealing and partitioning treatment parameters on the volume fraction, carbon enrichment, and stability of retained austenite in low-alloy TRIP-assisted steels. Specifically, we aim to (i) establish correlations between partitioning heat treatment conditions, phase fractions, and austenite stability, and (ii) evaluate the effect of these parameters on mechanical properties using in-situ high-energy X-ray diffraction (HE-XRD). Furthermore, a correlation between microstructural evolution, austenite stability, and deformation characteristics established.

sections.heading: Experimental procedure
paragraphs:
The model alloy employed in this study had a chemical composition of Fe–0.2C–1.6Mn–1.0Ni–1.4Si–0.5Al (in wt%). The equilibrium phase diagram, computed using Thermo-Calc software, is presented in  
                      Fig. 1 
                      a . The calculated critical transformation temperatures, A 3  and A 1 , were 868°C and 650°C, respectively, as indicated.  Fig. 1 
                      b  illustrates the predicted equilibrium phase fractions of ferrite (α) and austenite (γ) within the intercritical temperature range. These Thermo-Calc results were instrumental in formulating the suitable heat treatment strategies.

The alloy was synthesized through vacuum induction melting followed by casting. A schematic of the subsequent thermo-mechanical processing steps is shown in  
                      Fig. 2 
                      (a) . The cast ingot underwent austenitization at 1200°C for two hours, followed by hot rolling to a finish temperature of 800°C and air cooling. After descaling, the ingot was reduced to a final thickness of 15 mm, revealing a ferrite-pearlite microstructure, as depicted in  Fig. 2 
                      (b) . Subsequently, the hot-rolled plates were cold-rolled to a thickness of 1.5 mm, using lubrication and a controlled reduction of 5 % per pass. The cold-rolled microstructure, shown in  Fig. 2 
                      (c) , exhibited significant deformation in the ferrite phase, while pearlitic colonies experienced fragmentation, consistent with earlier observations  [34] . To refine the microstructure, the cold-rolled samples were subjected to recovery annealing a well-established technique for producing ultrafine grains  [34] ,  [35] . At this stage, the microstructure comprised partially recrystallized and recovered ferrite grains, with nano-sized cementite precipitates ( Fig. 2 
                      (d) ). Insets in  Fig. 2 b–d display grain boundary maps, distinguishing high-angle grain boundaries (>15°) and low-angle boundaries (2–15°). The resulting microstructure, containing ultrafine ferrite with dispersed cementite particles ( Fig. 2 
                      (d) ), served as the starting point for this investigation. A two-step heat treatment was applied post recovery annealing (as outlined in  Fig. 2 
                      (a) ). First, intercritical annealing was conducted at 750°C for 5 min in a salt bath furnace. Immediately after, the specimens were transferred to a second salt bath held at 400°C for isothermal partitioning, with dwell times of 1 min (PT1), 2 min (PT2), and 5 min (PT5), followed by water quenching at room temperature. A specimen (PT0) was quenched directly after intercritical annealing, without partitioning. Prior to each experiment, the furnace was allowed to stabilize for at least 20 min at the set temperature. The actual temperature fluctuations were continuously monitored using a K-type thermocouple immersed in the bath. The maximum deviation during holding was within ±2 °C for both annealing (750°C) and partitioning (400°C). This narrow deviation ensures reliable reproducibility of the microstructures obtained.

Microstructural characterization was performed using a field emission gun scanning electron microscope (FEG-SEM, JEOL 7100 F) equipped with an EBSD detector. The instrument was operated at 15 kV, and data analysis was carried out using TSL-OIM software. Sample preparation involved conventional metallographic grinding and mechanical polishing, followed by electropolishing in an electrolyte comprising 90 % ethanol and 10 % perchloric acid (vol%) at 22 V for 30 s at room temperature. Further substructural analysis was performed using scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM, JEOL 2100 F) operating at 200 kV. Thin foils for TEM were prepared using a twin-jet electro polisher with the same electrolyte, under 15 V at room temperature.

Uniaxial tensile testing was conducted on a universal testing machine (Shimadzu, Japan) at room temperature, using an initial strain rate of 8.3 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹ . The tensile specimens, with dimensions of 10 mm gauge length, 2.5 mm width, and 1 mm thickness, were extracted parallel to the rolling direction from the heat-treated sheets. Strain in the gauge region was measured using a macro-Digital Image Correlation (DIC) technique  [15] . To investigate the deformation-induced transformation of retained austenite, in-situ high-energy X-ray diffraction (HE-XRD) experiments were carried out during tensile testing at beamline BL46XU of the Super Photon Ring-8GeV (SPring-8), Hyogo, Japan. The monochromatic X-ray wavelength was 0.0413 nm, and the beam area irradiating the gauge section was 2 × 0.5 mm². A detailed description of the synchrotron setup is available in Ref.  [36] . The specimen geometry and strain rate matched those of the standard tensile test, with the exception of reduced thickness (∼0.5 mm) for the in-situ measurements. Phase fractions of ferrite, martensite, and retained austenite were quantified from the HE-XRD peak intensities using the method reported by Hossain et al.  [37] . Additionally, the martensite start temperature (M s ) was determined via differential scanning calorimetry (DSC, Shimadzu 600), with heating and cooling rates maintained at 2 °C/min.

sections.heading: Mechanical properties
paragraphs:
The engineering stress–strain curves obtained from static tensile tests for the PT0, PT1, PT2, and PT5 specimens are shown in  
                         Fig. 5 
                         a , and the corresponding mechanical properties are summarized in  
                         Table 2 . The PT0 specimen (as-quenched condition) exhibits the highest tensile strength of 1395 MPa but the lowest ductility, with a uniform elongation of 7.2 % and a total elongation of 11.6 %. Following intercritical annealing and partitioning at 400°C for 1 min (PT1), the tensile strength decreases to 1124 MPa, while the ductility improves significantly (uniform elongation: 14.6 %, total elongation: 18.9 %). Further partitioning for 2 min (PT2) and 5 min (PT5) leads to a continued reduction in tensile strength to 1054 MPa and 1006 MPa, respectively, accompanied by a progressive increase in ductility. The PT2 specimen achieves a uniform elongation of 16.8 % and a total elongation of 22.3 %, whereas PT5 exhibits the highest ductility among all conditions, with a uniform elongation of 20.5 % and total elongation of 27.6 %.

Fig. 5 
                         b  presents the strain hardening rate and true stress–true strain curves for all specimens. The PT0 condition shows a rapid drop in strain hardening rate, which is characteristic of dual-phase microstructures comprising ferrite and martensite. In contrast, PT1, PT2, and PT5 exhibit enhanced strain hardening behavior, with PT5 displaying the highest strain hardening rate sustained over a longer deformation range. This indicates a delayed onset of plastic instability in the PT5 specimen, which contributes to its superior uniform elongation. The mechanical performance observed in  Fig. 5  and  Table 2  is clearly influenced by the phase distribution and volume fractions in the microstructure. The highest strength in PT0 correlates with its high martensite content (∼40 %), while the increase in ductility is primarily associated with the volume fraction of retained austenite. Among all samples, PT5 contains the highest amount of retained austenite (∼20 %), while PT1 has the lowest (∼9 %). This correlation highlights the essential role of retained austenite in enhancing ductility through the TRIP effect. A better balance between strength and ductility is reflected in the product of tensile strength and total elongation (i.e., toughness index). PT5 achieves the highest value of 27.7 GPa·%, followed by PT2 (23.5 GPa·%), PT1 (21.2 GPa·%), and PT0 (16.2 GPa·%).

sections.heading: Transformation of retained austenite during deformation
paragraphs:
A series of in-situ tensile tests were conducted to study the change in retained austenite fraction during deformation.  
                         Fig. 6 
                         a  shows the HE-XRD (200) peak for austenite ( γ)  and (200) peak for ferrite ( 
                            α 
                         ) from the PT5 specimen, in the undeformed, as well as in deformed conditions, at 5 %, 10 %, 15 % and 20 % tensile strains. From  Fig. 6 
                         a  it is evident that, with increasing strain, the peak is shifted to lower theta region, which indicates increased lattice strains of  
                            α 
                          and  
                            γ 
                          during the deformation  [40] . Another important feature from  Fig. 6 
                         a  is that the peak becomes asymmetric and its intensity decreases in the case of ferrite. In the case of austenite, however, the peak intensity eventually becomes almost zero, indicating the activation of the TRIP effect, which causes the transformation of metastable austenite to martensite during deformation. The asymmetry in the BCC peak could be due to the evolution of deformation-induced martensitic phase, which can significantly be affected by solute carbon content, which further modifies the peak shoulder  [41,42] .

Fig. 6 
                         b  reveals the change in retained austenite fraction with nominal strain, in the PT1, PT2 and PT5 conditions. Before tensile deformation, the volume fractions of retained austenite were around 9 %, 12 % and 20 % in the PT1, PT2 and PT5 conditions respectively. During deformation, the retained austenite (RA) fraction progressively transformed into martensite in all partitioning conditions, consistent with the TRIP effect. However, the transformation kinetics differed between the three partitioning times, and these differences are already apparent at very small strains. At early deformation stages, when RA grains are not yet surrounded by martensite, the transformation rate primarily reflects the intrinsic stability of the individual RA grains. While the later-stage reflects strain localization and interaction effects. Overall, this stability is governed by their carbon enrichment, morphology, and size distribution, all of which depend on the partitioning treatment  [22] .

sections.heading: Discussion
paragraphs: Since intercritical annealing conditions were held constant in this study, the partitioning stage (here, the isothermal hold at 400°C) is the only processing variable and therefore the key driver of the observed differences in final microstructure and mechanical behavior; the largest change is seen between the unpartitioned (PT0) and partitioned specimens (PT1, PT2 and PT5), while increasing partitioning time progressively increases retained-austenite fraction and carbon enrichment (see  Table 1  and  Fig. 5 ). These two factors will ultimately determine how stable the retained austenite is going to be, so that the desired gradual TRIP effect will occur during deformation. It is envisaged to discuss these three aspects separately.

sections.heading: Microstructural changes occurring during partitioning
paragraphs: The as-quenched (PT0) specimen consists of 40 % martensite, which indirectly represents the fraction of retained austenite present at the intercritical annealing temperature (750 °C). Interestingly, when the two-stage treatment is applied, the volume fraction of austenite is found to decrease, depending on the isothermal holding time at 400 °C, from its value at the intercritical annealing temperature. Thus, decomposition of retained austenite takes place during partitioning treatment, with a concomitant change in the microstructure. For comprehensive microstructural observation, the PT5 specimen was chosen, which shows the highest volume fraction of RA (around 20 %) among the partitioned samples. Besides that, this sample is composed predominantly of ferrite and austenite, with only negligible amount of martensite.

Fig. 7 
                         a  shows the SEM image of a particular area of interest in PT5 condition.  Fig. 7 
                         b  shows the EBSD phase+IQ map and  Fig. 7 
                         c  represents the inverse pole figure (IPF) map of the same location, as in  Fig. 7 
                         a.  In  Fig. 7 
                         a to e,  region 1, region 2 and region 3 at specific locations were marked with dotted lines. Future discussion will concern these three areas only. In the above identified areas, the microstructure consists of only ferritic and austenitic grains. From the SEM image ( Fig. 7 
                         a ) it was noticed that two kinds of surface relief are often visible in the case of ferritic grains. For instance, in region 2, the center of the ferritic grain appears relatively smooth than the area near the grain boundary (pointed with arrow), which reveals a rougher surface. However, such kind of difference is not detectable in the phase map ( Fig. 7 
                         b)  as well as IPF map ( Fig. 7 
                         c ).

Fig. 7 
                         d  indicates the kernel average misorientation (KAM) map, in which misorientation between 0° to 4° can be recognized within the large ferrite grains. KAM map clearly shows that, in the selected three regions, relatively higher misorientation exists in the ragged boundary regions of the ferrite grains, than in the grain interiors. The misorientation difference between location to location has been indicated with a definite color on the grain boundary map ( Fig. 7 
                         e ). For instance, the ferrite grain belonging to region 2 consists of three different colors, in which each color represents misorientation between point to point, which is less than 2°. Although slight misorientation gradient does exist in a particular location of the grain, the overall deviation of misorientation within a grain is limited to ≤ 4°, and these have been represented in a (010)  α  pole figure ( Fig. 7 
                         f ).

Fig. 8 
                         (a,b)  reveal TEM micrographs of the PT5 specimen showing polygonal ferrite and retained austenite grains. It is observed that a typical dislocation cell structure forms near the ferritic grain boundary, while the interior seems to be free from dislocations. Therefore, it can be presumed that dislocation cell structure near the ferrite/austenite interface could be responsible for the evolution of misorientation gradient in the microscopic scale. It is worth mentioning that, the ferrite grains showing misorientation gradients, always share grain boundaries with the adjacent retained austenite grains ( Fig. 7  and  Fig. 8 ). During intercrtitical annealing, austenite is expected to nucleate at ferrite-cementite interfaces ( Fig. 2 
                         d ) and continue to grow. In the subsequent partitioning heat treatment, some of the austenite (FCC) formed during inter-critical annealing decompose into the ferritic (BCC) phase, as observed in SEM-EBSD and TEM studies.

This partitioning treatment process was intended to increase the carbon concentration in the austenite phase, so that it could be stabilized at RT. The present study indicates that there may be two possible mechanisms for carbon enrichment into austenite during the partitioning heat treatment. In the first case, decomposition of austenite into ferrite can progress by the migration of ferrite/austenite boundary, which will result in the growth of existing ferritic grains by consuming the adjacent austenite grains, without any nucleation event. The ferrite/austenite interface movement can be associated with long-range diffusion of carbon as well as very short-range diffusion of substitutional atoms. Generally, the interstitial carbon atoms have high mobility at 400 °C, whereas substitutional atoms can be considered to be rather immobile or stationary at that temperature. However, atom probe studies by multiple researchers have found out that during the partitioning treatment, the substitutional atoms like Mn  [43] , and Si  [44] , can diffuse very short distances along with the interface. These observations seem to support the results of the present investigation. For example, consider ferritic grains in region 1 and region 2, both the grains possess specific orientations, in which misorientation deviation exactly corresponds to the ragged nature of part of ferritic grains observed in SEM ( Fig. 7 
                         a  and  e ). Thus, it's presumed that, formation of ragged (rough) surface indicates the growth of intercritical ferritic grains, as a result of grain boundary migration. Similar kind of observation was reported by Speer and his coworkers in the case of quenching and partitioning steels, in which they observed grain boundary migration of martensite at the expense of austenitic grains during partitioning  [45,46] . Based on this understanding, the schematic ( Fig. 7 
                         g  and  h ) was drawn to represent the interpreted microstructure at the inter critical annealing stage (full grain of austenite), and after partitioning treatment, when area of austenite grain decreased with simultaneous growth of ferrite.

The growth of ferrite by the migration of the ferrite/austenite interface may not happen in all the locations. This will become amply clear by comparing the behavior of regions 1 and 2, on one side, and region 3 on the other. In regions 1 and 2, each of the central ferritic grains belongs to one main orientation and their surfaces also consist of both smooth and rough patches. By contrast, in region 3, there is no evidence of any smooth surface at all and only shows a rough portion. This can be explained by assuming that part of the austenitic areas transforms displacively into carbide free bainite of similar composition, when inter-critical austenite is quenched at the partitioning temperature of 400 °C. Then, during isothermal holding, due to the higher activity, carbon can diffuse from bainitic ferritic grains into the closest austenitic grains, resulting in carbon enrichment in the latter  [47] .  Fig. 7 
                         i  shows the schematic illustration of region 3, in the intercritical state and also after partitioning. Although the mechanisms of formation of ferrite from austenite are quite different in the two cases, the appearance of the newly formed ferrite would be of similar substructure. Thus, partitioning heat treatment is a crucial step, in order to control grain size, carbon content and volume fraction of the retained austenite phase.

sections.heading: Enrichment of carbon into austenite during partitioning
Determination average carbon concentration in austenite
paragraphs: In the present study, the stabilization of the austenitic phase occurs in two steps. Most importantly, during intercritical annealing, austenite can be stabilized by the enrichment of Mn, Ni and C  [24,48] . At a later stage, during partitioning treatment, austenite can be further stabilized by carbon atoms, which becomes available from the ferritic transformation. In the present study, intercritical annealing temperature and time are fixed, and the only variable parameter is the isothermal holding time at 400 °C. In this range hardly any substitutional diffusion can occur. Hence, it is expected that in all the studied specimens, only the carbon concentration will differ, depending on the partitioning kinetics. Therefore, it is essential to evaluate the level of carbon enrichment of the austenite during partitioning, which will control the austenitic stability.

Fig. 9 
                            a  shows the variations in the average carbon content of austenite and its lattice parameter in PT1 (1 min. holding), PT2 (2 min. holding) and PT5 (5 min. holding) conditions. It is clear from this figure that during isothermal holding at 400 °C, the lattice parameter of austenite and its average carbon concentration both increase as the holding time increases. The increase in lattice parameter can be understood as, during the partitioning stage, carbon will diffuse from the transforming austenite, (which becomes ferrite after the transformation), by rejecting the extra carbon atoms inside the austenitic grains, and this causes slight expansion in the austenitic lattice. Few earlier studies also reported this effect  [50,51] . Furthermore, the PT1 and PT2 conditions show average carbon concentrations of 1.01 and 1.07 wt% respectively, the PT5 specimen shows carbon concentration around 1.10 wt%. The carbon content of austenite, at the intercritical temperature, as estimated by the Lever rule, was 0.5 wt% only. Thus, carbon concentration in austenite could be greatly enhanced by the partitioning heat treatment.

sections.heading: Thermal stability of retained austenite
paragraphs:
The stabilization of austenite against martensitic transformation is closely related to its carbon content. In order to determine the thermal stability of retained austenite against martensitic transformation, DSC technique was utilized.  Fig. 9 
                            b  shows the typical DSC peaks obtained for partitioned specimens having PT1, PT2 and PT5 conditions. From  Fig. 9 
                            b,  it is observed that there is a single exothermic peak in the case of PT5 condition, within the temperature range of −32.3 °C to −42.2 °C. This indicates the decomposition of austenite into martensite, where the temperatures −32.3 °C and −42.2 °C are related to the martensite start (M s ) and the martensite finish (M f ) temperature, respectively. The higher carbon concentration (1.10 wt%) of PT5 specimen improves the stability of austenite, and this significantly decreases the martensite start temperature to below room temperature  [52] . On the other hand, PT1 and PT2 specimens show multiple exothermic peaks, at different temperature regions. It appears that, instead of a single M s  temperature, PT1 specimen shows M s  temperature at −10.7 °C and −30.0 °C, and PT2 specimen shows M s  temperature at −14.7 °C and −31.2 °C. This signifies that the retained austenite, in these two cases, certainly possesses a varied range of stability. In fact, it has been suggested that carbon distribution can be inhomogeneous, in the retained austenite grains, at different locations. For instance, Xiong et al.  [53] , who used atom probe tomography, reported that the variation of carbon content in different retained austenite grains may be caused due to their different morphologies (film-type or blocky-type), as influenced by the neighboring phases. Again, Onuki et al., who pursued in-situ neutron diffraction experiments, observed that the heterogeneity of carbon concentration among retained austenite grains arose due to insufficient partitioning kinetics at 400 °C  [53] . Therefore, it will be quite reasonable to link the M s  temperature of retained austenite with its thermal stability.

A close look at the central austenite grain in  Fig. 8 (a), the visible section of the austenite grain surrounded by ferrite appears ∼1 μm across in the TEM foil; however, the actual three-dimensional grain size may be larger.

Thus, when ferritic grains on opposite sides of the austenite grain invade it during PT5 condition, there is ample opportunity for the carbon atoms to travel from the periphery to the central region of the austenite grain. As will be shown in  
                            Fig. 10 , the average retained austenite grain sizes for the conditions PT1, PT2 and PT5 are rather similar and vary within the range 0.78 µm to 0.83 µm. Thus, it is quite obvious that homogeneous carbon distribution in retained austenite is very much possible under the PT5 condition. However, this will not be true in cases PT1 and PT2, where the carbon concentration is bound to be inhomogeneous. This explains why the PT5 specimens end up with a microstructure of ferrite and austenite only, while the martensite phase additionally occurs in the PT1 and PT2 specimens. These results are also consistent with the DSC results, shown in  Fig. 9 (b).

sections.heading: Stability of retained austenite and TRIP effect
paragraphs: It is well known that the stability of retained austenite is dictated mostly by its carbon content, in lean composition TRIP-assisted steels  [8] . Here, the term ‘stability’ does not imply that retained austenite resists transformation indefinitely. Instead, it refers to the controlled, gradual transformation of carbon-enriched RA embedded in ferrite, which delays strain localization and sustains work hardening. Although carbon concentration of a steel undoubtedly has a strong influence, this alone cannot account for the retention of 10–20 vol percent of austenite in the final microstructure. In this connection, the effects of grain size and shape as well as of the phases surrounding the retained austenite, should also be considered.

sections.heading: Grain size and shape
paragraphs: The average grain sizes of retained austenite in PT1, PT2 and PT5 specimens are similar and the mean value varies between 0.78 µm to 0.83 µm. The distribution of grain sizes, acquired from the EBSD grain map ( Fig. 10 a), also show a similar trend. For grain size measurements, the high angle grain boundaries (greater than 15°) were chosen for the calculations. A number of studies  [25,56]  indicated that grain size is inversely proportional to the stability of retained austenite, such that finer austenite grains are relatively more stable than coarser austenitic grains. Finer austenite grains have higher interfacial energy per unit volume and hence require a larger driving force for martensitic transformation. Again, in all conditions, the morphology of retained austenite appears mostly of "blocky" shape, and few austenitic grains possess "lath" (film) shape.

As mentioned earlier, retained austenite grains in the PT5 specimen are mostly surrounded by the ferrite phase, with at most a trace of pre-existing martensite. However, in the case of PT1 and PT2 specimens, the retained austenite is surrounded by both ferrite and martensite. The steel samples in the PT1 and PT2 conditions have around ∼22 % and ∼12.7 % martensite, respectively. The characteristics of martensite are known to depend on the carbon content  [42] . By using a carbon balance approach, we estimated the average carbon content in martensite existing in the PT1 and PT2 specimens.

This explains how RA can be simultaneously described as ‘stable’ in the microstructural sense and yet fully transformed at higher strain levels.

sections.heading: Influence of TRIP effect on mechanical properties
paragraphs: The crucial test of compositionally lean TRIP-assisted steels is that these steels must achieve improved crashworthiness, by simultaneous enhancement of strength and ductility. Thus, a strategy to improve the strain hardening ability of low alloy steels is the key aspect in the development of advanced high strength steels  [1,59] . The PT0 (as quenched) specimen shows the highest strength due to large volume fraction of martensite (around 40 %), which results in substantially low elongation. It exhibits higher work hardening rate at the initial plastic strains, and these later decreases steeply with the applied strain, resulting in the lowest uniform elongation ( Fig. 5 ). The greater work hardening rate of PT0 specimen at initial plastic strains is due to its basic dual phase nature, in association with ferrite and martensite. The steep decrease of work hardening rate at later stages may be due to incompatible accommodation of stress and strain distribution between ferrite and martensite. This will cause formation of micro voids and then cracks can initiate near the interface, leading subsequently to damage nucleation processes  [60] .

On the basis of this investigation, it is clear that by using industrially feasible two step heat treatment (intercritical annealing + partitioning treatment), it is possible to produce an optimum volume fraction of retained austenite (around 20 %, as in the PT5 condition) in a lean steel, which is not usual in conventional low alloy steels  [39] . Normally, the addition of ‘Ni’ can help to increase retained austenite fraction to such an extent  [61] . However, the present results suggest that, it is possible to increase the volume fraction of retained austenite by increasing the partitioning time at 400 °C, while keeping stability of retained austenite more or less intact. In view of not too dissimilar range of stability of retained austenite, in the PT1, PT2 and PT5 specimens, it is worthwhile to compare their observed mechanical properties. The present study shows that, increasing the volume fraction of retained austenite increases the strength-ductility (UTS Χ TEL) synergy in studied steel ( Table 2 ). The PT5 specimen shows the highest combination of strength-ductility, which derives from the TRIP effect. During deformation, retained austenite undergoes strain induced martensitic transformation. The role of the newly formed martensite can be twofold, 1) it may strengthen local regions and suppress the micro level cracks and void formation, and 2) like in dual phase steel (PT0), it can contribute to the overall work hardening, as a result of which, uniform elongation increases. In addition to that, the newly formed martensite phase will exert a compressive stress on the retained austenite, due to volume expansion, and consequently, the critical stress required for transformation of austenite to martensite will increase. The aforementioned mechanisms can operate simultaneously and, therefore, it is quite complex and difficult to determine their relative effectiveness. In fact, the PT1 and PT2 specimens also show significant uniform elongation as a result of the TRIP effect. Since these two specimens consist mostly of ferrite and martensite and rather low fractions of retained austenite, these show lesser extent of TRIP effect. The present data indicate that UTS scales primarily with the pre-existing martensite fraction, whereas RA chiefly controls uniform/total elongation through the TRIP effect. From PT1→PT2→PT5 the sequential reduction of initial α′ (≈21–23 % → ≈12–13 % → trace) explains the non-linear drop in UTS (1124 → 1054 → 1006 MPa) despite the monotonic increase in RA (≈9 % → ≈13 % → ≈20 %). Thus, TRIP is most effective at a phase balance where a limited amount of martensite provides baseline strength and ∼15–20 % RA supplies sustained work-hardening; the optimum strength–ductility product in this study occurs in PT5. From the present and past results it is also clear that, the volume fraction of martensite is more sensitive to increasing the strength of steel, whereas, retained austenite fraction is more sensitive to improving uniform elongation  [62,63] . The present study suggests that microstructural design for adjusting the volume fractions of ferrite and martensite and by maintaining retained austenite fraction at around 20 %, may lead to better mechanical properties in the future generation advanced high strength steels with lean composition.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs:
In this study, the microstructural evolution and mechanical properties of a lean-alloyed TRIP-assisted multiphase steel were systematically investigated after intercritical annealing at 750°C and subsequent partitioning treatment at 400 °C for different holding times (0, 1, 2, and 5 min). The major conclusions are as follows: 
                         
                            1. 
                            The directly quenched specimen (0 min) exhibited the highest martensite fraction (∼40 %). Partitioning for 1 min and 2 min reduced the martensite fraction (∼21 % and ∼13 %, respectively) and increased the retained austenite fraction (∼9 % and ∼13 %). Prolonged partitioning for 5 min yielded a ferrite+austenite structure with ∼20 % retained austenite and only a trace of martensite. 
                         
                         
                            2. 
                            During partitioning, a fraction of intercritical austenite transformed into ferrite by interface migration and bainitic transformation. The stabilization of the remaining austenite was achieved primarily through carbon enrichment (confirmed by synchrotron-based lattice parameter analysis) and grain refinement. Although this mechanism is well established, our results quantify its kinetics under short-time partitioning in a lean alloy. 
                         
                         
                            3. 
                            Retained austenite in all partitioned specimens progressively transformed into martensite during deformation, providing strain hardening through the TRIP effect. In-situ synchrotron HE-XRD revealed that the transformation rate was strongly influenced by the amount of pre-existing martensite and by stress partitioning with the surrounding phases. 
                         
                         
                            4. 
                            The ultimate tensile strength (UTS) scaled with the pre-existing martensite fraction (1124 → 1054 → 1006 MPa for 1 min → 2 min → 5 min), whereas uniform and total elongations were governed by the fraction and stability of retained austenite (18.9 % → 23.4 % → 27.6 % total elongation). The optimum balance was achieved after 5 min partitioning, where ∼20 % stable retained austenite sustained the TRIP effect despite reduced martensite content. This demonstrates that strength–ductility synergy is maximized when ∼15–20 % stable retained austenite coexists with a limited amount of martensite. 
                         
                         
                            5. 
                            The specimen partitioned for 5 min showed the better strength–ductility synergy (UTS ∼1006 MPa, total elongation ∼27.6 %). Although the absolute elongation values may be slightly overestimated due to the short 10 mm gauge length (a limitation imposed by synchrotron in-situ testing requirements), the trends are robust, and strain measurement by DIC minimized this effect.
